# Azure Dns Resolver management client library for .NET

Microsoft Azure Dns Private Resolver enables you to query Azure Dns private zones from an on-premises environment and vice versa without deploying VM based Dns servers.

This library supports managing Microsoft Azure Dns Resolver resources.

This library follows the [new Azure SDK guidelines](https://azure.github.io/azure-sdk/general_introduction.html), and provides many core capabilities:

    - Support MSAL.NET, Azure.Identity is out of box for supporting MSAL.NET.
    - Support [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) for distributed tracing.
    - HTTP pipeline with custom policies.
    - Better error-handling.
    - Support uniform telemetry across all languages.

## Getting started 

### Install the package

Install the Azure Dns Resolver management library for .NET with [NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/):

```dotnetcli
dotnet add package Azure.ResourceManager.DnsResolver
```

### Prerequisites

* You must have an [Microsoft Azure subscription](https://azure.microsoft.com/free/dotnet/).

### Authenticate the Client

To create an authenticated client and start interacting with Microsoft Azure resources, see the [quickstart guide here](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-net/blob/main/doc/dev/mgmt_quickstart.md).

## Key concepts

Key concepts of the Microsoft Azure SDK for .NET can be found [here](https://azure.github.io/azure-sdk/dotnet_introduction.html).

## Documentation

Documentation is available to help you learn how to use this package:

- [Quickstart](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-net/blob/main/doc/dev/mgmt_quickstart.md).
- [API References](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/?view=azure-dotnet).
- [Authentication](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-net/blob/main/sdk/identity/Azure.Identity/README.md).

## Examples

Code samples for using the management library for .NET can be found in the following locations
- [.NET Management Library Code Samples](https://aka.ms/azuresdk-net-mgmt-samples)

## Troubleshooting

-   File an issue via [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-net/issues).
-   Check [previous questions](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/azure+.net) or ask new ones on Stack Overflow using Azure and .NET tags.

## Next steps

For more information about Microsoft Azure SDK, see [this website](https://azure.github.io/azure-sdk/).

## Contributing

For details on contributing to this repository, see the [contributing
guide][cg].

This project welcomes contributions and suggestions. Most contributions
require you to agree to a Contributor License Agreement (CLA) declaring
that you have the right to, and actually do, grant us the rights to use
your contribution. For details, visit <https://cla.microsoft.com>.

When you submit a pull request, a CLA-bot will automatically determine
whether you need to provide a CLA and decorate the PR appropriately
(for example, label, comment). Follow the instructions provided by the
bot. You'll only need to do this action once across all repositories
using our CLA.

This project has adopted the [Microsoft Open Source Code of Conduct][coc]. For
more information, see the [Code of Conduct FAQ][coc_faq] or contact
<opencode@microsoft.com> with any other questions or comments.

decisions.reason: The Custom partial defines this public factory, and lines 30-45 implement precisely the conditional nested-property construction and list normalization cited. A model factory is a reusable generator-addressable shape; the claimed historical motivation is not necessary to establish the observed behavior.

Lines 52-72 show the factory signature, tags fallback, conditional nested model, endpoint-list materialization, and extra name argument. The proposal describes this handwritten factory body without inferring an unobserved wire behavior.

The Custom factory adds a public single-WritableSubResource signature and forwards it to the separately supplied handwritten model constructor. It is an additional model-factory entry point, distinct from the constructor's null check and property assignment.

The signature and forwarding call on lines 88-90 demonstrate the nullable wrapper-to-identifier conversion and argument reorder. This factory overload adapts its input, separately from the identifier overload's model construction.

The second DnsResolverData factory overload visibly defaults tags and conditionally wraps virtualNetworkId in SubResource while constructing DnsResolverProperties. Its signature/body and citation distinguish it from the wrapper-input forwarding overload.
Lines 119-134 show a handwritten public factory with tags normalization, a four-input condition, and a materialized domains list inside the nested properties. The citation covers the exact behavior.
Lines 141-156 supply the factory signature and conditional InboundEndpointProperties construction, including tags and IP-configuration list defaults. This is a separate public model-factory behavior.
The optional WritableSubResource overload on lines 163-165 forwards subnet?.Id with reordered etag to the other handwritten factory overload. The description stays within this visible adapter.

The identifier-taking overload on lines 172-187 defaults tags and conditionally creates properties with a SubResource. This is the constructor-assembly counterpart to, not a duplicate of, the wrapper-taking adapter.

The public Custom factory on lines 194-207 visibly defaults tags and conditions its nested policy properties on the two nullable inputs. The model-factory pattern is reusable without treating the comment about migration as independently verified history.

Lines 214-216 show a distinct wrapper-input factory overload extracting virtualNetwork?.Id and delegating with reordered arguments. The claim does not attribute implementation of the identifier-based nested model to this overload.

The identifier-based policy-link factory on lines 223-236 visibly defaults tags and conditionally creates the nested link properties. The cited method is separate from the wrapper-input overload and has the proposed shape.

Lines 243-263 show unconditional DnsSecurityRuleProperties construction, an action wrapper, two list conversions including the empty managed list, and tags normalization. This is handwritten model-factory assembly; no service response or generated implementation is assumed.

The non-generated helper on lines 10-26 converts two optional string inputs into one nullable MatchConditions object and constructs ETags only for non-null inputs. It is a reusable input-shape normalization used by several handwritten adapters, not evidence of custom LRO or service policy.

The two hidden public collection overloads on lines 20-31 adapt string preconditions and delegate to typed overloads; the returned ArmOperation alone does not imply a custom poller. Both sync/async forms implement the same compatibility behavior.

The ruleset collection's sync and async bodies use the shared precondition conversion before delegating, preserving the other arguments. This is one handwritten legacy overload family rather than separate polling or serialization behavior.

Lines 20-31 show matching sync/async network-link creation adapters from separate string conditions to MatchConditions. The concrete delegation supports the proposed category, symbols, and legacy-overload pattern.

The resolver collection defines both handwritten overloads and forwards via CompatibilityRequestConditions.Create with the other arguments intact. The observation does not require verifying the historical generated signature.
The domain-list collection's sync/async CreateOrUpdate methods visibly convert both optional precondition strings and delegate. The cited lines identify one compatibility-overload behavior.

Bulk and BulkAsync on lines 20-31 forward to their MatchConditions variants after converting the string pair. The source does not implement batching or polling here, so the convenience/legacy-overload classification is appropriate.

The inbound-endpoint collection contains the cited hidden sync/async overload pair and forwards converted preconditions to other CreateOrUpdate methods. The proposed symbols and range match this handwritten compatibility behavior.

The outbound-endpoint collection's two cited methods implement a single string-condition overload family and preserve all other arguments while delegating. This is not a custom LRO despite the ArmOperation return type.

The method and CodeGenSuppress do show a handwritten identifier-helper replacement, but the catalog already has backward-compatibility-shim for retained changed public APIs. The original new pattern emphasizes URI construction rather than the specifically documented preservation of a named-argument-compatible parameter name; that historical explanation is only a source comment, not independently established.

limitations: Eighteen captures from 263 eligible source files were supplied; eight named Custom files were skipped. No package-wide absence or exhaustive discovery claim is made.

Source comments describe AutoRest/TypeSpec migration, prior parameter names and released APIs, but generated counterparts, the prior release baseline and specification bodies were not supplied; those historical and causal claims remain unverified.

The shared precondition helper returns null for two null strings. Callers merely delegate after packing inputs; WaitUntil/ArmOperation do not establish custom polling, and Bulk does not implement a local batching loop.

Factory null guards test aggregate input absence, not service validity. No nullable Value dereferences appear in these factories. Tags/default lists, conditional property bags, the ruleset factory's additional name argument and unconditional security-rule action/list construction are reported literally without assigning meaning to unnamed null/default constructor slots.

The three WritableSubResource forwarding factory overloads and three identifier-construction overloads are distinct supplied signatures/behaviors. Forwarding wrappers preserve null via ?.Id; the separate public data constructors explicitly reject null wrappers where shown.

The ruleset list constructor accepts null as an empty list. The other visible wrapper constructors do not locally validate wrapper Id, and the resource-ID helpers contain no explicit escaping or argument guards.

The extension's mockable ArmClient and VirtualNetworkDnsResolverResource implementations are named skips. Their caching, scope validation and operation behavior are not independently inferred; security-rule model construction is not an authentication or security-enforcement implementation.

Coverage is partial: 18 captured Custom source files out of 263 eligible files, with eight named Custom files omitted for budget. Neither unprovided source nor library-wide absence of further customizations can be assessed.

No generated counterpart, released baseline, or implementation of the mockable ArmClient and virtual-network wrapper was supplied. Source comments describe compatibility motivation, but cannot independently establish prior API signatures, generated equivalence, or service causes.

The 30 proposed instances account for the distinct visible factory methods, precondition conversion and overload families, identifier-helper replacements, model constructors, and ArmClient extension in the captured files; no distinct uncited behavior was identified within those files. Generator addressability is a plausibility judgment, not a demonstrated generator capability.
